summary: A percentage is a number of parts per hundred — a standardised proportion — so it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45). Because a percentage is relative to its whole (base), the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts, and percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half wholes). Standardising 'out of 100' is what makes percentages useful for comparing proportions with different totals. Teaching grounds the definition in a 100-grid, drills the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confronts the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.
misconceptions: Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount (50% is 'the same amount' regardless of the whole), not as a proportion of its base
Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is seen as a maximum rather than 'one whole')
Confuses 'A as a percentage of B' with 'B as a percentage of A', or which quantity is the whole (the base)

activities.title: Shade a 100-grid to define 'per hundred'
steps: On a 10×10 grid (100 cells, each cell = 1%), shade 45 cells and write the result three ways: 45% = 45/100 = 0.45.
State in your own words what '45 out of 100' means by pointing at the shaded and unshaded parts of the grid.
Shade a second grid partly to show more than one whole: fill one full grid and 50 cells of a second, and write 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes.
Convert a small percentage carefully: shade 7 cells and record 7% = 7/100 = 0.07 (watch that it is 0.07, not 0.7).
activities.insight: A percentage literally means parts per hundred, so it is the same quantity expressed as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal; 100% is 'one whole', not a ceiling, and percentages can go beyond it.

activities.title: Same percentage, different wholes — 50% of two bags
steps: Predict first: Bag A has 20 sweets and Bag B has 40 sweets. If you take 50% of each, will you get the same amount from both, or more from one — and why? Write your reason before checking.
Shade half of two bars (or grids) sized to represent 20 and 40, and compare the shaded amounts.
Explain in one sentence why the same percentage gave different amounts.

Check a trap comparison: is 100% of a small 10-sweet bag more or fewer sweets than 50% of Bag B (40 sweets)? Compute both (10 and 20): 50% of the larger bag gives MORE than 100% of the smaller bag — so '100% always beats 50%' is false, because each percentage acts on its own whole.
activities.insight: A percentage is a proportion of its own whole (50% = half of whatever the whole is). Because the wholes differ, equal percentages give different amounts, so a percentage is not a fixed absolute quantity; a larger whole's 50% can even exceed a smaller whole's 100%.

activities.title: Convert fluently between fraction, decimal and percentage
steps: Match each percentage to its decimal and its fraction-out-of-100 (e.g. 45% ↔ 0.45 ↔ 45/100; 7% ↔ 0.07 ↔ 7/100; 150% ↔ 1.5 ↔ 150/100).
Go in both directions: given 0.08, write the percentage (8%); given 3/100, write the percentage (3%) and decimal (0.03).
Place a given value on a number line that passes 100%, locating 150% at one and a half wholes.
Explain the decimal-placement rule: converting a percent to a decimal divides by 100, moving two places, so a small percent becomes a small decimal (7% → 0.07).
activities.insight: The three forms are interchangeable notations for the same proportion; converting reliably in both directions depends on tracking the 'out of 100' divisor and decimal place.

activities.title: Express one quantity as a percentage of another, and compare
steps: Write 'A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, and say aloud 'A out of B, restated out of 100'.
Compare two results: one class had 18 out of 25 pass, another 70 out of 100. Convert 18/25 to a percentage (72%) and decide which class did better.
Explain why percentages make this comparison easy: both are restated out of the same total, 100.
Check direction: is 'A as a percentage of B' the same as 'B as a percentage of A'? Try A=10, B=40 (10/40×100 = 25% vs 40/10×100 = 400%) and state which quantity is the whole each time.
activities.insight: Standardising to 'per hundred' lets you compare proportions with different totals; the base (the 'of B' quantity) is the whole, and swapping A and B changes the question and the answer.

checkQuestion: Bag A has 20 sweets and bag B has 40 sweets. Is 50% of bag A the same amount of sweets as 50% of bag B? And — this is the important part — how do you know?
checkAnswer: No. 50% of bag A is 10 sweets and 50% of bag B is 20 sweets. A percentage is a proportion of its OWN whole (50% means half of whatever the whole is), so because the bags have different totals, the same percentage gives different amounts.
